name: Curcumin
explanation: Yellow colour from turmeric. No safety concern at permitted levels.

name: Riboflavin
explanation: Vitamin B2 used as a yellow colour. Safe.

name: Tartrazine
explanation: Synthetic azo dye. In the EU, foods containing it must carry a warning that it 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'.

name: Quinoline yellow
explanation: Synthetic dye that requires the EU 'activity and attention in children' warning. EFSA lowered its ADI in 2009.

name: Sunset yellow FCF
explanation: Synthetic azo dye with the mandatory EU warning about activity and attention in children.

name: Carmine
explanation: Red colour made from insects, so it is not vegan or vegetarian. It can cause allergic reactions in rare cases.

name: Carmoisine
explanation: Synthetic azo dye with the mandatory EU warning about activity and attention in children.

name: Ponceau 4R
explanation: Synthetic azo dye with the mandatory EU warning about activity and attention in children. EFSA lowered its ADI in 2009.

name: Allura red AC
explanation: Synthetic azo dye with the mandatory EU warning about activity and attention in children.

name: Brilliant blue FCF
explanation: Synthetic blue dye. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI; it adds colour only, no nutrition.

name: Chlorophylls
explanation: Natural green pigment from plants. Safe.

name: Copper chlorophyllin
explanation: Green colour made from chlorophyll. Safe at permitted levels.

name: Plain caramel
explanation: Brown colour made by heating sugar. Safe.

name: Ammonia caramel
explanation: Caramel colour made with ammonia. Can contain small amounts of 4-MEI, a by-product EFSA set limits for.

name: Sulphite ammonia caramel
explanation: The most common caramel colour (in colas). Can contain 4-MEI; EFSA considers it safe within limits.

name: Vegetable carbon
explanation: Black colour from charred plant material. EFSA noted data gaps on possible contaminants.

name: Carotenes
explanation: Orange pigment, the same family as the pro-vitamin A in carrots. Safe as a food colour.

name: Annatto
explanation: Orange-yellow colour from achiote seeds. Safe at the ADI; rare allergic reactions are reported.

name: Paprika extract
explanation: Red-orange colour from paprika. Safe.

name: Beetroot red
explanation: Red colour from beetroot. Safe.

name: Anthocyanins
explanation: Purple-red pigments from fruit and vegetables. Safe.

name: Calcium carbonate
explanation: Chalk, used as a white colour, anti-caking agent or calcium source. Safe.

name: Titanium dioxide
explanation: White pigment that is no longer allowed in food in the EU since 2022 because EFSA could not rule out genotoxicity. Still permitted in some other countries.

name: Iron oxides
explanation: Mineral pigments (red, yellow, black). Safe at permitted levels.

name: Sorbic acid
explanation: Prevents mould and yeast. Safe at permitted levels.

name: Potassium sorbate
explanation: Common mould inhibitor in bars and shakes. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI.

name: Benzoic acid
explanation: Preservative. Safe at the ADI, but some people are sensitive to benzoates, and children who consume a lot can approach the ADI.

name: Sodium benzoate
explanation: Preservative used in drinks. Combined with vitamin C it can form traces of benzene; some sensitive people react to benzoates.

name: Sulphur dioxide
explanation: Preservative that can trigger reactions in people with asthma or sulphite sensitivity. Must be declared as an allergen above 10 mg/kg.

name: Sodium metabisulphite
explanation: Sulphite preservative; can trigger reactions in people with asthma or sulphite sensitivity.

name: Nisin
explanation: Natural antimicrobial peptide from bacteria. Safe at permitted levels.

name: Sodium nitrite
explanation: Curing agent in processed meat (e.g. protein jerky). It can form nitrosamines; EFSA says exposure is within safe limits but processed meat itself is linked to colorectal cancer.

name: Potassium nitrate
explanation: Curing agent that converts to nitrite. See E250.

name: Acetic acid
explanation: The acid in vinegar. Safe.

name: Lactic acid
explanation: Acid naturally produced by fermentation. Safe.

name: Carbon dioxide
explanation: The gas in fizzy drinks. Safe.

name: Malic acid
explanation: Fruit acid that adds sourness. Safe.

name: Ascorbic acid
explanation: Vitamin C, used to stop oxidation. Safe.

name: Sodium ascorbate
explanation: A salt of vitamin C. Safe.

name: Ascorbyl palmitate
synonyms: fatty acid esters of ascorbic acid
explanation: Fat-soluble form of vitamin C that protects oils from going rancid. Safe.

name: Tocopherol-rich extract
explanation: Natural vitamin E that protects fats from oxidation. Safe.

name: Alpha-tocopherol
explanation: Vitamin E. Safe.

name: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA)
explanation: Synthetic antioxidant. EFSA keeps it authorised at a low ADI; it is classified as a possible human carcinogen by IARC (2B).

name: Butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)
explanation: Synthetic antioxidant authorised at a low ADI. EFSA considers current exposure safe.

name: Citric acid
explanation: Fruit acid used for tartness and as a preservative aid. Safe.

name: Sodium citrates
explanation: Salt of citric acid, stabilises proteins in shakes. Safe.

name: Potassium citrates
explanation: Salt of citric acid. Safe.

name: Calcium citrates
explanation: Salt of citric acid, also a calcium source. Safe.

name: Tartaric acid
explanation: Grape acid. Safe.

name: Rosemary extract
explanation: Natural antioxidant from rosemary. Safe at permitted levels.

name: Phosphoric acid
explanation: Adds sharpness (colas). EFSA set a group ADI for phosphates in 2019; high consumers and people with kidney disease should limit intake.

name: Sodium phosphates
explanation: Keeps proteins smooth in shakes and processed cheese. Covered by EFSA's 2019 phosphate group ADI; heavy use adds up across processed foods.

name: Potassium phosphates
explanation: Common in ready-to-drink protein shakes. Covered by EFSA's phosphate group ADI; relevant for people with kidney disease.

name: Calcium phosphates
explanation: Anti-caking agent and calcium source. Covered by EFSA's phosphate group ADI.

name: Diphosphates
explanation: Phosphate additive. Covered by EFSA's phosphate group ADI.

name: Triphosphates
explanation: Phosphate additive. Covered by EFSA's phosphate group ADI.

name: Polyphosphates
explanation: Phosphate additive. Covered by EFSA's phosphate group ADI.

name: Alginic acid
explanation: Thickener from seaweed. Safe.

name: Sodium alginate
explanation: Seaweed-derived thickener. Safe.

name: Agar
explanation: Seaweed gel, a vegan alternative to gelatin. Safe.

name: Carrageenan
explanation: Seaweed thickener used in shakes and dairy alternatives. EFSA (2018) kept it authorised but asked for more data and set a temporary ADI; some people report gut discomfort.

name: Processed Eucheuma seaweed
explanation: Less refined form of carrageenan. Same caveats as E407.

name: Locust bean gum
explanation: Thickener from carob seeds. Safe.

name: Guar gum
explanation: Thickener from guar beans, also a soluble fibre. Safe; large amounts can cause bloating.

name: Gum arabic
explanation: Tree resin used as a thickener and fibre. Safe.

name: Xanthan gum
explanation: Fermentation-made thickener. Safe.

name: Tara gum
explanation: Thickener from tara seeds. Safe.

name: Gellan gum
explanation: Fermentation-made gelling agent that keeps particles suspended in shakes. Safe.

name: Pectin
explanation: Fruit fibre used as a gelling agent. Safe.

name: Cellulose
explanation: Plant fibre. Safe, but it adds bulk without nutrition.

name: Methyl cellulose
explanation: Modified cellulose used as a binder. Safe.

name: Hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose
explanation: Modified cellulose used as a binder and in capsules. Safe.

name: Carboxymethyl cellulose
explanation: Modified cellulose thickener. EFSA sees no safety concern, but animal and small human studies suggest effects on gut bacteria; research is ongoing.

name: Lecithins
explanation: Emulsifier from soy, sunflower or rapeseed that helps powders mix. Safe. Soy lecithin must be labelled as a soy allergen.

name: Polysorbate 80
explanation: Synthetic emulsifier. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI; animal studies suggest possible effects on the gut lining and microbiome.

name: Polysorbate 60
explanation: Synthetic emulsifier. Similar caveats to polysorbate 80.

name: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
explanation: Very common emulsifier. EFSA (2017) sees no safety concern, but it can contain process contaminants (glycidyl esters, 3-MCPD) and is a marker of ultra-processing.

name: DATEM
synonyms: mono- and diacetyl tartaric acid esters
explanation: Emulsifier used in baked goods. Safe.

name: Sucrose esters of fatty acids
explanation: Emulsifier. Safe at the ADI.

name: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids
explanation: Emulsifier. Safe.

name: Polyglycerol polyricinoleate
explanation: Emulsifier that makes chocolate coatings flow. Safe.

name: Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate
explanation: Emulsifier. Safe at the ADI.

name: Sorbitan monostearate
explanation: Emulsifier. Safe at the ADI.

name: Sodium carbonates
explanation: Baking soda. Safe; adds a little sodium.

name: Potassium carbonates
explanation: Used to alkalise cocoa. Safe.

name: Ammonium carbonates
explanation: Raising agent that evaporates during baking. Safe.

name: Magnesium carbonates
explanation: Anti-caking agent and magnesium source. Safe.

name: Calcium chloride
explanation: Mineral salt. Safe.

name: Calcium sulphate
explanation: Used to set tofu. Safe.

name: Sodium hydroxide
explanation: Used in tiny amounts to adjust acidity; neutralised in the food. Safe.

name: Silicon dioxide
explanation: Keeps powders free-flowing. EFSA (2018) found no safety concern at reported uses but noted data gaps, especially on nano-sized particles.

name: Calcium silicate
explanation: Anti-caking agent. Safe.

name: Talc
explanation: Anti-caking agent; EFSA re-evaluation pending more data.

name: Magnesium salts of fatty acids
explanation: Flow agent in powders and tablets. Safe.

name: Glucono-delta-lactone
explanation: Mild acid made from glucose. Safe.

name: Monosodium glutamate
explanation: Savoury flavour enhancer. EFSA (2017) set a group ADI that high consumers of processed food can exceed.

name: Disodium guanylate
explanation: Flavour enhancer usually paired with MSG. Safe.

name: Disodium inosinate
explanation: Flavour enhancer usually paired with MSG. Safe.

name: Beeswax
explanation: Coating made by bees, so not vegan. Safe.

name: Carnauba wax
explanation: Plant wax that makes coatings shiny. Safe.

name: Shellac
explanation: Resin made by lac insects, so not vegan. Safe.

name: Nitrogen
explanation: Inert gas used in packaging. Safe.

name: Nitrous oxide
explanation: Propellant in whipped toppings. Safe.

name: Sorbitol
explanation: Sugar alcohol. EU labels must warn that 'excessive consumption may produce laxative effects'; about 20 g at once can cause bloating or diarrhoea.

name: Mannitol
explanation: Sugar alcohol with a strong laxative effect in amounts around 20 g.

name: Glycerol
explanation: Keeps bars soft. Safe; very large amounts can cause headaches or loose stools. It has calories but often isn't counted as sugar.

name: Isomalt
explanation: Sugar alcohol; laxative effects in larger amounts.

name: Maltitol
explanation: Sugar alcohol common in 'low sugar' bars. It raises blood sugar about half as much as sugar and is one of the polyols most likely to cause gas and diarrhoea.

name: Lactitol
explanation: Sugar alcohol made from milk sugar; laxative in larger amounts.

name: Xylitol
explanation: Sugar alcohol that is good for teeth but laxative in larger amounts. Highly toxic to dogs, so keep products away from pets.

name: Erythritol
explanation: Best-tolerated sugar alcohol with almost no calories. EFSA (2023) set an ADI of 0.5 g/kg body weight; some observational studies link high blood levels to cardiovascular events, which is still being studied.

name: Acesulfame K
explanation: Intense sweetener, about 200 times sweeter than sugar. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI.

name: Aspartame
explanation: Intense sweetener. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI (40 mg/kg); IARC classified it as 'possibly carcinogenic' (2B) in 2023. Not suitable for people with phenylketonuria (PKU).

name: Cyclamate
explanation: Intense sweetener with a low ADI (7 mg/kg). Banned in the USA; allowed in the EU in limited uses.

name: Saccharin
explanation: Oldest intense sweetener. EFSA raised its ADI in 2024 and considers it safe.

name: Sucralose
explanation: Intense sweetener used in most protein powders. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI; recent lab studies on a by-product (sucralose-6-acetate) and on heating have prompted further review.

name: Thaumatin
explanation: Sweet protein from the katemfe fruit. Safe.

name: Steviol glycosides
explanation: Plant-derived intense sweetener. EFSA considers it safe at the ADI.

name: Neotame
explanation: Intense sweetener related to aspartame, used in tiny amounts. Safe at the ADI.

name: Aspartame-acesulfame salt
explanation: Combination of aspartame and acesulfame. Not suitable for people with PKU.

name: Advantame
explanation: Very intense sweetener used in tiny amounts. Safe at the ADI.

name: Polydextrose
explanation: Synthetic fibre used to replace sugar. Counts as fibre on the label, which lowers 'net carbs'; large amounts can cause bloating.

name: Acetylated distarch adipate
explanation: Modified starch. Safe, but a marker of processing.

name: Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate
explanation: Modified starch. Safe, but a marker of processing.

name: Propylene glycol
explanation: Carrier for flavourings and moisture keeper. Safe at the ADI.

name: Natural flavouring
explanation: Flavour extracted from natural sources. Regulated and safe, but the exact substances don't have to be disclosed.

name: Flavouring
explanation: Unspecified flavourings. Every flavouring substance is assessed by EFSA, but labels don't say which ones are used.

name: Enzymes
explanation: Enzymes added to aid digestion or processing (for example lactase to break down lactose). Safe.
